title: Is the Word Hidden in the Grid?

concept.title: Follow the letters, and free the cell when the road ends
body: A word is hidden in a grid if you can walk from cell to cell (up, down, left or right) so that the cells spell the word, and **no cell is used twice**. Try every cell as the start. From a cell that matches the current letter, try the four neighbours for the next letter. A cell used on the current road is marked, and **unmarked when the search leaves it**, because another road may use it.

The check of the letter happens **first**, so a road is cut at the first wrong letter. That is why the search is fast in practice: a word of length `L` has at most `4 * 3^(L-1)` roads from one cell, and most of them are cut long before the end. As soon as one road succeeds, all the callers return `True` and nothing else is explored.

statement: A grid of lowercase letters and a word are given. The word is *in the grid* if its letters can be found in order in cells that are neighbours (above, below, left or right of each other) and no cell is used more than once. Decide whether the word is in the grid.
inputFormat: Each of the next `r` lines has `c` letters.
The last line has the word.

examples.note: The road a(0,0), b(0,1), c(0,2), c(1,2), e(2,2), d(2,1) spells abcced.

hints: Start a search from every cell.
Check the letter first: a wrong letter ends this road at once.
Mark the cell before trying the neighbours and unmark it afterwards.

starter.python:
r, c = map(int, input().split())
grid = [input().strip() for _ in range(r)]
word = input().strip()

explanation: A search starts from every cell. It fails at the first wrong letter, succeeds when the last letter matches, and otherwise marks the cell, tries the four neighbours for the next letter, and unmarks the cell. Success is passed up at once.
solution.complexity: Time O(r * c * 4 * 3^(L-1)) in the worst case, usually far less; space O(r * c).
